import { Aside, Steps, CardGrid, LinkCard } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

Once your app compiles, it still has to become something a node can install.
That deliverable is an **`.mpk` bundle**: a single archive carrying your
`calimero:app` component, a `manifest.json`, and an Ed25519 signature.
This page walks the builder workflow that produces one.

Every step is a `meroctl app` subcommand: `build` compiles the components, `signer`
makes the signing key, `pack` writes the manifest, signs it and packs the
archive, and `inspect` checks the result as a node would. The node
side — how a bundle is parsed, verified, and trusted on install — lives in
[Upgrades & migration](/protocol/upgrades/); this page does not duplicate that
detail.

<BuildAppPipeline />

## The workflow

<Steps>

1. **Build the component.**

   `meroctl app build` compiles your crate for `wasm32-wasip2` and turns it into a
   `calimero:app` component, with the ABI the SDK's macros embed (its
   `calimero:abi` section). `meroctl` comes with each release, beside `merod`
   ([Install](/operate/install/)).

   ```bash
   meroctl app build apps/my-app --out my-app.wasm
   ```

   A WASM core module (an SDK 0.12 app) is refused by the node
   (`400 UNSUPPORTED_BUNDLE`).

2. **Generate a signing key (one-time).**

   `meroctl app signer new` creates an Ed25519 keypair and derives your **signer
   id** — a `did:key` identifier built from the public key (the `0xed01`
   ed25519-pub multicodec tag plus the 32-byte key, base58btc-encoded under the
   `did:key:` prefix).

   ```bash
   meroctl app signer new my-signing-key.json
   # Generated new keypair: my-signing-key.json
   #   signerId: did:key:z6Mkrb81NKkv7Mw4dZAWA5PTuwBhbq9u9eCPuby3icBUdirg
   ```

   The key file is JSON with base64url-encoded `private_key` and `public_key` plus
   the derived `signer_id` (`meroctl app signer id <file>` prints it
   again). `signer new` will not overwrite an existing file unless you pass
   `--force`, which loses the old key for good. **Keep it secret and out of version control** — it is
   your update authority (see below).

   <Aside type="caution">
   For local development you can sign with the built-in well-known dev key via
   `meroctl app sign <manifest> --dev` instead of `--key` (`meroctl app pack`
   uses it when `--key` is left out). A dev-signed bundle is
   marked as such, **cannot be published to the registry**, and is refused
   (`403 DEV_SIGNED_PACKAGE`) by a node not running with `--dev` or
   `--allow-unsigned-bundles` — use a generated key for anything real.
   </Aside>

3. **Write and sign the manifest, and create the `.mpk`.**

   `meroctl app pack` writes `manifest.json` (`version`, `package`,
   `appVersion`, `minRuntimeVersion` and the `app.wasm` artifact with its SHA-256
   and size), signs it, and packs `manifest.json` and
   `app.wasm` into a gzip-compressed tar. Signing derives the `signerId` from
   the key, refuses to sign if `minRuntimeVersion` is absent (a signer must not
   rewrite the document it signs), canonicalizes the manifest with RFC 8785 (JCS),
   signs the domain-tagged SHA-256 of those canonical bytes, and writes a
   `signature` object back into the manifest.

   ```bash
   meroctl app pack --wasm my-app.wasm --package com.example.my-app \
     --app-version 1.0.0 --key my-signing-key.json --out dist/com.example.my-app-1.0.0.mpk
   # omit --key to sign with the development key
   meroctl app inspect dist/com.example.my-app-1.0.0.mpk   # verify it as a node does
   ```

   Given the crate's directory instead, `meroctl app pack apps/my-app --key
   my-signing-key.json` reads `package`, `min-runtime-version` and `frontend-dir`
   from the crate's `[package.metadata.calimero]` and the release from its
   `version`, builds the components when `--wasm` and `--compute` are not given,
   and writes `apps/my-app/dist/<package>-<version>.mpk`. The same table gives
   the display `metadata` (`name`, `description`, `author`, `icon`, `tags`,
   `license`, `category`, `guide`), `handlers.slug`, `links` (`frontend`,
   `github`, `docs`) and `frontendAliases`, and the crate's `calimero-sdk` git
   dependency gives `buildInfo` (`sdkSource`, `sdkVersion`: the SDK it was built with).

   `--min-runtime-version` (default `0.1.0`) is the oldest `merod`
   release the app needs; a cluster with an older replica refuses the upgrade
   (`409 RUNTIME_TOO_OLD`). For every release after the first, pass
   `--previous <last .mpk>`: `pack` then compares the two ABIs, warns about
   changes that break callers, and refuses a state change made without a state
   version bump ([App interface](/build/app-abi/#check-a-new-version-against-the-last)).

   The other fields a release may carry:

   | Flag | Manifest field | |
   | --- | --- | --- |
   | `--frontend <dir>`, `--frontend-entry <file>` | `frontend` | the app's static web build, served by the node ([Ship a frontend](/build/guides/frontends/)) |
   | `--outbound <https prefix>` (repeatable) | `outbound` | URL prefixes a run may send requests under ([Call an external service](/build/guides/outbound/)) |
   | `--upgrades owner\|publisher` | `upgrades` | who upgrades the package's instances; absent means `owner` |
   | `--guests allowed\|forbidden` | `guests` | whether an instance's listed accounts reach it without joining its organization; absent means `forbidden` ([Guests](/protocol/organizations/#guests)) |
   | `--instance-org standalone\|org\|either` | `instanceOrg` | which organization an instance is created in: one made with it, one its creator is in, or either; absent means `either` ([Where an instance goes](/protocol/organizations/#where-an-instance-goes)) |

   `pack` checks each against the node's own rules before signing.

   One more comes only from the crate's `[package.metadata.calimero]`:

   - `uses`: the other apps the release calls, by the name its code knows each by.
     Each names the package, the semver range it works with, and `mode`:
     `create` (the default) is created with the app and upgraded with it,
     `attach` is an app the deployer already runs. A `calimero.lock` beside
     `Cargo.toml` pins each to a release inside its range and to that release's
     ABI digest; `pack` writes both into the manifest and checks the vendored
     ABI (`calimero/abi/<name>.json`) against the digest. Without a lock the
     references are packed unpinned, with a note.

     ```toml
     [package.metadata.calimero.uses]
     kv = { package = "com.calimero.confidential-kv", range = "^0.1", mode = "create" }
     calendar = { package = "com.example.calendar", range = "^2", mode = "attach", methods = ["listEvents", "createEvent"] }
     ```

     `methods` lists what the release calls on that app as the person its run
     serves, once that person grants it
     ([As the person](/protocol/xcall/#as-the-person)); without it the release
     calls the app as itself. `pack` checks each against the vendored ABI.

     A node refuses a release whose references break the rules (`400 BAD_USES`:
     names `a-z0-9_`, at most 16, not its own package, a semver range, a locked
     version inside it, an ABI digest `sha256:<hex>`, at most 64 distinct method
     names, none of the node's own `__`). It lists them on the
     release's capability card, and an upgrade's consent page names the apps the
     new release starts using or uses differently.

     Creating an instance of a release with `create` references first creates
     each of them: in the same organization, by the same owner, from the release
     its lock pinned (else the newest installed one inside its range), among the
     installed releases the creator may use, those signed by the same key as
     the instance's own package, and, for an instance from a deployment, those
     the same deployment offers; a package with none answers
     `409 USES_NOT_INSTALLED`, as for a package that is not installed at all,
     named `<instance>.<name>`. The
     instance's record names them (`links`), the create answers them, and an
     `init` that takes a `links` parameter is told their ids:

     ```rust
     #[app::init]
     pub fn init(links: Option<BTreeMap<String, String>>) -> app::Result<Self> { .. }
     ```

     `links` in `initArgs` is the node's; a client that sends it is refused.
     `attach` references are never created.

     The instance and its members are one unit. An instance created from a
     deployment's offer gives each member the same deployment, which need not
     offer the member's release when the same key signed it (the instance's
     offer covers the unit): every member's usage is billed to the deployment's developer, and
     the deployment's secret values fill what the member's own release
     declares, as they do the instance's. Deleting the
     instance deletes every member with it, down to the members' own members
     (`DELETE /apps/{app}` answers them in `members`), and a member is not
     deleted alone while its instance stands (`409 UNIT_MEMBER`). Both wait
     for every node to run 1.0.0-rc.32 (`409 FEATURE_NOT_ACTIVE`).

     <UnitModel />

     The two modes side by side: a `create` member is part of its instance's
     unit, an `attach` link points at an app that stays its owner's own.

     The owner attaches an app they already run to an `attach` reference with
     `PUT /apps/{app}/links/{name} { app }` (whoever manages both apps, in one
     organization, with a passkey; `DELETE` detaches it). The app must run the
     reference's package (`409 WRONG_PACKAGE`); one outside the range is attached
     anyway, answered `inRange: false`, and an upgrade's consent page warns when
     the new release takes an attached app in another range: an attached app lives
     on its own and is never upgraded with the instance. Deleting the attached app
     detaches it. `GET /apps/{app}/links` lists every reference of the release the
     app runs with the app linked under it, the release that app runs and
     `inRange`. The app's code reads a link at any time, not only in `init`:

     ```rust
     let kv = env::linked("kv").ok_or_else(|| Error::NoKv.into())?;
     ```

     A member names the instance that created it with `env::unit_of()` (`None`
     for an app created on its own): Confidential KV and Private Inference
     releases take `app:<env::unit_of()>` as their admin, so the instance uses
     them with no grant step.

     A unit upgrades in one consent: an app's frontend asks the node's consent
     page with `upgradeUnit { app, toVersion }` (every app's sheet on one page),
     or a client calls `POST /apps/{app}/upgrade-unit { version }`
     (`meroctl` and the clients: `upgrade_unit`) moves the instance to `version`
     and each member to the release the new one pins for it (else the newest
     installed one in range), with one passkey assertion over the instance, its
     version and every member's target. It answers an upgrade run, followed with
     `GET /orgs/{org}/upgrades/{run}`. A member is not moved on its own off the
     range its instance takes it with (`409 OUTSIDE_UNIT_RANGE`), and a new
     release that creates a member the instance does not have is refused: a unit
     gains members only when it is created.

   A package of several services (each app instance runs one of them, named by
   `meroctl instance create --service NAME`) gives each with `--service
   NAME=PATH`, where PATH is the service's crate directory (built) or its
   component; the manifest then declares `services` instead of `wasm`:

   ```bash
   meroctl app pack --service directory=crates/directory --service room=crates/room \
     --package com.example.rooms --app-version 1.0.0 --key my-signing-key.json
   ```

   Or list them in the crate's table, paths relative to it, and `meroctl app pack
   DIR` packs them with no flags (`--service` replaces the list). A workspace
   root with no `[package]` of its own is read from `[workspace.metadata.calimero]`,
   its release from `[workspace.package] version`, and its services build into
   one target directory:

   ```toml
   [workspace.metadata.calimero]
   package = "com.example.rooms"
   services = [
     { name = "directory", path = "crates/directory" },
     { name = "room", path = "crates/room" },
   ]
   ```

   Each service is packed as `services/<name>.wasm`, with its compute component
   (built from its crate, or `--service-compute NAME=FILE` beside a component) as
   `services/<name>.compute.wasm` and its pipelines (`--service-pipeline
   NAME=FILE`) under `services/<name>/pipelines/`. A name is 1 to 64 letters,
   digits, `-` or `_`. `--wasm`, `--compute` and `--pipeline` pack one service and
   are refused beside services.

   An app with compute methods also builds a compute component
   (`meroctl app build <crate> --out app.wasm --compute-out compute.wasm`). Pass it
   with `--compute compute.wasm`: the manifest then declares it as `compute`, and
   the `.mpk` carries it as `compute.wasm`. Without it a release cannot run
   compute, and neither can a raw `.wasm` upload. `--compute` without `--wasm`
   packs a package with only a compute component.

   A release may also ship pipelines over its compute methods: `--pipeline
   daily.yaml` (repeatable) packs each file as `pipelines/<name>`, and the
   manifest lists it under `pipelines` (at most 16 per package, each at most
   64 KiB), signed with the rest. The node compiles each file at install and
   checks it against the package's own compute methods and the cluster's pools:
   the module is `self` (or left out) or another installed package by its exact
   name, optionally pinned (`module: com.acme.pdf@0.1.0`; without a version, the
   newest release the installer may pin). That package must ship a compute component;
   its methods and caps are the ones the step is checked against. A module is pinned
   only from a release the installer may use that is public or the operator's, signed
   by the package's own signer, or, for a release installed private, private to every
   organization the release is for; anything else, or a module with no compute
   component, is `UNKNOWN_MODULE`. An install of the same release again (for another
   organization, or public) keeps its pins and is refused the same way when a pin no
   longer meets that rule, so it never widens who runs a private module. The release
   keeps running the module release it was installed against until the pipeline's
   own package is released again. The module's package cannot be uninstalled while
   such a release exists (`409 MODULE_IN_USE`). The step's files, payer and usage
   stay the calling app's. Every method must be one its module
   declares, and each step's limits may only lower the method's caps. A problem
   is `400 BAD_PIPELINE` with `details`, a list of `{file, path, code, message}`
   for every error. A release with pipelines installs only once every node runs
   this release (`409 CLUSTER_NOT_UPGRADED`). `meroctl app pipelines PACKAGE`
   prints what a version registered.

4. **Install it.**

   A real cluster installs releases from its operator's registry
   (`POST /packages/install { package, version }`); publish the `.mpk` there
   with `meroctl app publish dist/com.example.my-app-1.0.0.mpk`: it pushes to the
   app registry (`--registry`) with the registry's API key (`--api-key` or
   `CALIMERO_REGISTRY_API_KEY`), or with `--org ORG` as a Calimero Cloud
   organization, whose API key it trades for a publish token. A new package is
   private unless `--public` lists it. A public registry refuses a dev-signed
   bundle.
   A development cluster (`merod --dev`, and `merod local`, which
   `meroctl local up` starts) also takes an
   upload:

   ```bash
   meroctl app install --path dist/com.example.my-app-1.0.0.mpk
   meroctl instance create --name my-app --package com.example.my-app --alias my-app
   ```

   Before it logs the install, the node checks the publisher's signature and
   every artifact's digest, `minRuntimeVersion`, the package's pinned signer
   (the first release's), and that each component prepares and imports only
   what the `calimero:app` world offers. Installing is what *produces* an
   application: the manifest's `package` and `signerId` fix the application id.
   A WASM that a release of another signer's package already ships is refused
   (`409`).

</Steps>

## Check a release before you ship it

`meroctl app check` says what the people running your app will see when this
release replaces the last one, with the same classifier the node uses for the
upgrade sheet (`calimero_bundle::update`):

```bash
meroctl app check --mpk release.mpk --against last.mpk
```

```
com.acme.notes 1.3.0 → 1.4.0
  Data can go to: https://inference.near.ai/v1/
  Users on automatic updates: wait for an owner's or admin's approval (green, but the app or the apps it created can send data out; only an update whose unit sends nothing out applies on its own)
  New methods: pin, unpin · removed: none · state version unchanged (1)
  Egress added: none · removed: none
  Signer: did:key:z6Mk… (unchanged)
```

The first line after the versions lists every destination outside Calimero the
release and the apps it creates may send data to, or says `Data: stays in
Calimero` when there is none. Any destination outside Calimero is just a
destination: the platform never vouches for an external endpoint, a TEE
included. If your app trusts one (a private-inference service, say), verify its
attestation in your own code; it is still listed.

The next line says what an organization that lets updates apply on their own
(`autoApply: noDestinations`, [Updates that apply on their
own](/protocol/upgrades/#updates-that-apply-on-their-own)) would see: only a
green release of an app whose unit sends nothing out, before or after, applies
on its own, after the hold, and it moves the app alone: the apps it created stay
on the releases they run until an owner or admin moves the unit. A green
release that can send data out still waits for an owner's or admin's approval.

A release is **red**, and waits for a person's approval, when it is signed by
another key, can send data somewhere new, declares another state version,
creates or drops an app that has egress, or newly calls another app's methods as
the person; each reason is listed. `--against VERSION` reads the installed
release from a node instead of a file, and the apps a release creates with
`uses` come from `--uses-mpk FILE` (or that node).

In a release workflow, run it before `app publish` (and before `app release`)
as a gate, so a destination never appears by accident: `--fail-on egress`
fails when egress grows, `--fail-on red` on any red reason, and
`--allow-egress PREFIX` is the pull request saying a new destination is meant.
It exits `0` when the gate passes, `1` when it fails, and `2` when it cannot
judge.

```yaml
- name: What users will see
  run: |
    meroctl app check --mpk dist/release.mpk --against dist/last.mpk \
      --fail-on egress $ALLOW_EGRESS   # e.g. "--allow-egress https://api.acme.com/" from the PR
```

## The signer key is the update authority

For a bundle, the application id is derived from the `package` **and** the
`signerId` together — not from the bytecode. That makes the application id
**version-stable**: a new release signed by the *same* key under the *same*
package keeps the same application id and is recognized as an upgrade of the
existing app.

The corollary is the rule to remember: **a new signed version must use the same
signer key.** Sign a new release with a different key and the node computes a
different application id — it is a *different application*, not an upgrade, and
existing contexts will not pick it up. Treat the signing key as the long-lived
identity of your app and guard it accordingly.

<Aside type="note" title="Every install path requires a signature">
There is one rule, not a per-path split: a bundle must carry a valid Ed25519
manifest signature to be installed, whether it comes from a registry, a URL, or
a local file. Dev builds are not an exception - they sign with the well-known
dev key (`meroctl app sign --dev`) and are verified like any other bundle; since
that key's seed is public, only a development node (`--dev` or
`--allow-unsigned-bundles`) installs a release it signed. The
signature also binds the wasm bytes: each wasm artifact is checked against the
SHA-256 the signed manifest records for it. The exact verification rules are
documented in [Upgrades & migration](/protocol/upgrades/).
</Aside>
